lesson.grammar_point: inversion after negative and limiting adverbials (not only, never, only when, at no point)

listenings.text: When I hire a new finance chief, I tell them the same thing on the first morning. Under no circumstances do I expect a plan in the first week. In fact, I would be worried if I got one. Rarely does a new person understand a business in five days, however good they are. What I want instead is a list of questions. Who are the people I need to meet? Where does the money really come from? Which processes does the team complain about? Only when those questions have answers do I want to talk about changes. The best finance chief I ever hired spent his whole first month in meetings, and at no point did he ask me for more time.

My first town hall as a finance director was a disaster, and I still remember every minute of it. I had been in the job for three days. I stood up in front of eighty people and presented five changes to the month-end close. Never have I seen a room go so quiet. Nobody asked a single question. Later, my controller told me why: the team had built that process themselves, and they heard about my changes at the same time as everyone else. In my next job, I did it differently. Not only did I wait a month before the first town hall, but I also met every team leader first. The changes were almost the same. This time, people asked when we could start.

extra_audio.text: On Monday, Fernando arrives for his onboarding and meets the chief executive. Next, he reads the handover notes from the interim CFO. In a one-to-one, Beatriz tells him about the bottleneck in the month-end close. At the town hall on Thursday, he says that only when he has taken stock will he talk about changes. Finally, he promises to come back in a month and show the team what they did.

reading.rtitle: The first week: what new finance chiefs wish they had known
paras: Ask finance chiefs about their first week in a new company and most of them describe the same pressure: everybody expects them to hit the ground running. The chief executive wants a view on the numbers, the board wants a date for the plan, and the team wants to know whether their jobs are safe.

The ones who did well resisted that pressure in public. Not only did they avoid announcing changes at the first town hall, but they also told the team why: they had not yet taken stock. One of them said that only when she had held a one-to-one with every manager did she feel ready to talk about priorities.

Several described the same mistake from an earlier job. They had arrived with a fresh pair of eyes, spotted a bottleneck in the month-end close on day two, and fixed it on day three. The fix was right, but morale fell, because nobody had been asked. At no point, they admitted, had they thought about how it looked to the people who had built the process.
Their advice is simple. Use the onboarding period to listen, read the handover notes twice, and make one small promise you can keep. You earn trust in weeks, not in a speech.
reading.source: Adapted from interviews with newly appointed finance chiefs

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: A new finance chief should fix every problem in the first week, because the whole team expects a fast start from day one.
New finance chiefs do better when they listen and take stock before they announce changes.
